### Prerequisites

Before you continue, review the two texts this lesson builds on: **On Equality**, where we learned what it means to compare, and **Natural limits**, where a limit was defined as a maximum, a minimum, or an approximation. Here we join both ideas and turn them into one rule you can use

### Introduction

The texts on equality taught us to decide whether two things are equal. But equality alone is not enough: when two things — or two numbers — are not equal, we still need to say which one is greater and which one is smaller, and later measure how much they differ. This text prepares the tools for that: the symbols of comparison, a scale that uses them, and the language of limits.

Reflection 1: I am going to use...?

We already saw that there is a symbol for equality (=). Should we use the same symbol to say that something is greater or smaller?

### The Rule of Greater and Smaller

A rule tells us how to act in a given situation: it says what we should do, and it stays the same every time that situation appears. The rules of a game tell us what counts as a point; the rules of a calendar tell us how the days are organized. Mathematics works the same way: before we compare or calculate, we agree on how to read what we write, and that agreement is a rule.

We have already used one such rule: the texts on equality taught us that the symbol (=) states when two values are the same. The rule of this text tells us which of two numbers is greater and which is smaller.
Figure 1: A centesimal scale: it runs from 0 to 100 in equal steps.

Figure 1 is a ruler: the straight, marked strip we use to measure length. Here, however, it measures values instead. The long marks carry the numbers 0, 10, 20 and so on until 100, and the shorter marks between them stand for the values in between. Because every mark is equally spaced from its neighbours, each value from 0 to 100 has its own place on the ruler, and we can point to it.

Look at Figure 1: the numbers we studied earlier are listed in order. When a number comes **after** another, it is **greater**. We write that relationship with the symbol (>), so *21 > 20* means "21 is greater than 20"
The opposite is also true: a number that comes **before** another is **smaller**. We use the symbol (<), so *20 < 21* means "20 is smaller than 21"

A useful tip: the open side of the comparison symbol — greater (>) or smaller (<) — always faces the larger number. Test it with *21 > 20*: the opening faces 21.

When the gap between the two numbers is huge, mathematics offers a shortcut: (≫) reads "much greater than", as in *1000000 ≫ 20*, and (≪) reads "much less than", as in *20 ≪ 1000000*

Practice

An inequality is a statement that must stay true. If you change one side, you have to change the other side in the same proportion, or the comparison breaks. Try it yourself: use the arrows to move the hands up and down, and watch how both numbers change together:

### Using the Rule on a Scale

The ruler in Figure 1 is already a scale: it begins at a minimum of 0 and ends at a maximum of 100, and the distance from one mark to the next is always the same. To use it as a measuring tool, we only have to decide what each of those marks is worth. If we want to count how many of ten characteristics an object has, we can give each characteristic ten marks: the first one carries the reading from 0 to 10, the second from 10 to 20, and so on until the tenth, which brings it to 100.

Measuring then becomes something we can watch on the ruler. We go through the list of characteristics one by one: every characteristic the object has pushes the reading that many marks to the right, and every characteristic it lacks leaves the reading where it is. Where the reading stops is the score of the object.

Because the marks are equally spaced, the place where the reading stops already tells us how the object did. A reading close to 100 sits near the maximum, so the object has almost every characteristic we asked for; a reading close to 0 sits near the minimum, so it has almost none. We often write this measurement as a percent (symbol "%"), reading the marks of the ruler as parts out of a hundred: 90% is the reading at the mark 90, and 10% is the reading at the mark 10.

Two objects can now be compared by looking at where each one stops on the same ruler. Since the marks grow from left to right, the reading further to the right is the greater one: *90% > 10%*, because 90 comes after 10. In the following texts we will put this ruler to work, comparing objects by the scores they get.

### Conclusion

In this text we learned the rule of comparison. With the symbols (>) and (<) we can say which of two numbers is greater and which is smaller — the open side of the symbol always faces the larger number. Table 1 showed that an inequality must stay true: when one side changes, the other has to change in the same proportion. We then used the rule on a centesimal scale, where scores move toward the maximum of 100 as objects match the defined characteristics and toward the minimum of 0 as they deviate.
